title: Prints with a Purpose: 'America Today' Exhibition Amplifies Artists' Voices
summary: In a time of political turbulence, art can be a megaphone. The Print Center in Philadelphia presents 'America Today: Voices in Contemporary Print,' an exhibition running through July 25 that features 37 artists who use printmaking to engage with urgent societal issues. Timed with the nation's 250th anniversary, the show explores fundamental principles like the common good, civil rights, and social justice. The prints—drawn from six renowned printmaking workshops across the U.S.—are as varied in style as the topics they address. From community histories to systemic violence, the works make a crucial contribution to conversations about our collective past, present, and future. The participating studios are not just production sites; they are vital gathering places that foster community and support artists as outspoken advocates. They include Brandywine Workshop and Archives (Philadelphia), Coronado Print Studio (Austin), Crow's Shadow Institute of the Arts (Pendleton, OR), EFA Robert Blackburn Printmaking Workshop (New York), Self Help Graphics & Art (Los Angeles), and Women's Studio Workshop (Kingston, NY). Among the exhibiting artists are Natalie Ball, whose work often confronts Native identity; Chakaia Booker, known for her textured explorations of race and ecology; and Howardena Pindell, a pioneer in addressing racism and feminism. Other participants include Cannupa Hanska Luger, Wendy Red Star, and Marie Watt, each bringing distinct perspectives. The exhibition, supported by The Pew Center for Arts & Heritage, underscores printmaking's democratic power—the ability to produce multiple copies allows art to reach wider audiences. As the nation grapples with its identity, these prints serve as both mirrors and provocations. Visit printcenter.org for more details.
why_it_matters: This exhibition shows that art isn't just decoration; it can challenge injustice and bring communities together, inspiring young people to use their own creativity to speak out on issues they care about.

background_read: The Print Center in Philadelphia is one of the oldest nonprofit spaces in the United States dedicated to photography and printmaking, founded in 1915. It has long been a hub for artists experimenting with print techniques.

The exhibition coincides with the nation's 250th anniversary (the semiquincentennial in 2026), a moment that often sparks reflection on the ideals of the Declaration of Independence and the continuing struggle for equal rights and justice.

Printmaking has a storied history as a tool for activism. During the 1960s, for example, artist Emory Douglas created powerful posters for the Black Panther Party using screenprinting, making art cheaply reproducible and hard to ignore.

Several participating workshops have deep community roots. Self Help Graphics & Art, founded in 1970 in East Los Angeles, has long supported Chicano and Latino artists. The EFA Robert Blackburn Printmaking Workshop was named after a Jamaican-born master printmaker who championed diversity in the arts.

Artist Howardena Pindell, featured in 'America Today,' was a trailblazer: she worked as a curator at the Museum of Modern Art, helped found the feminist A.I.R. Gallery, and has used her abstract paintings and videos to confront racism and sexism since the 1970s.

perspectives.description: The exhibition amplifies the voices of artists from marginalized communities and turns gallery walls into a forum for civic dialogue. By showcasing diverse perspectives, it reminds the public that art can be a force for social change.

Art exhibitions risk becoming echo chambers, mainly reaching audiences who already agree with the messages. Critics argue that symbolic representation alone does not address deep-rooted inequality, and that systemic change requires action beyond gallery spaces.

The show fits into a long tradition of using printmaking as a democratic medium, dating back to woodcuts during the Reformation and protest posters of the 20th century. Today's artists build on that legacy while tackling contemporary problems like racial inequality and nationalism.

If exhibitions like this inspire young artists to engage with accessible media, printmaking could see a revival as a tool for activism. It might also push museums and schools to integrate such works into curricula, widening the conversation about what it means to be American.
